newsitem.title: USA: US debt futures end lower ahead of US retail sales.
newsitem.headline: US debt futures end lower ahead of US retail sales.

text.p: U.S. debt futures closed slightly lower in one of the thinnest sessions of the year, as traders bided their time ahead of Tuesday's U.S. June retail sales data.
September T-bonds dipped towards the bottom of their narrow ranges at the close, but traders and analysts said the market's performance was impressive in light of skyrocketing grain prices.
"Even though commodity prices were higher today, the long-term trend is very negative," said Barrett Lewald, senior financial futures strategist at Lind-Waldock Inc.
September T-bonds traded to 113-29/32 at the close, near the daily low of 113-28/32, but held above last Friday's low of 113-23/32.

Traders said September T-bonds were consolidating before breaching the seven-month high of 114-15/32, which was set on Friday and roughly corresponds to the key support level of 6.50 percent in the U.S. long bond.
Long-term weakness in commodity prices is not only diminishing expectations of a higher rate of U.S. inflation, but lifting the specter of deflation, they said.
"With crude oil at the lower end of its trading range and gold prices at 12-year lows, it would be difficult for me as a Fed member to raise rates," Lewald said.
Expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will keep U.S. interest rates unchanged have contributed to the lack of volatility in the U.S. bond futures market, they said.
Aside from several 1,000-lot trades, the T-bond futures pit was quiet and sparse. Several large local traders were absent, floor sources said.
Lewald said the market is vulnerable to a downside correction if U.S. June retail sales rise more than expected.
Economists surveyed by Reuters are looking on average for a 0.2 percent rise in retail sales and an increase of 0.5 percent in sales excluding automobiles.
The BTM/Schroders weekly retail sales data will be released at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, 30 minutes after the U.S. retail sales data.
One analyst said a stronger than expected U.S. employment cost index, which is scheduled for release on July 29, could also ignite a corrective selloff.
However, most traders and analysts see September T-bonds rising to 118-00, which roughly corresponds to 6.375 percent.
Lewald expects September to hit 121-00 or about 6.25 percent in the longer term.

At the end of pit trade, September T-bonds were off 06/32 at 113-30/32, 10-year notes were down 04/32 at 109-14/32, December Eurodollars were 0.03 lower at 94.04, and muni bonds were off 04/32 at 119-12/32.
